clinicalPearls: Tamponade is a clinical and haemodynamic diagnosis, not merely an echocardiographic one; a pericardial effusion of any size compressing the heart may cause tamponade if it accumulates faster than the parietal pericardium can stretch.

The rate of accumulation matters more than absolute volume: rapid bleeding of a small volume (e.g. after cardiac perforation or aortic dissection) can be fatal, whereas a slowly accumulating chronic effusion may exceed a litre before compromise.
Beck's triad (hypotension, muffled heart sounds, raised jugular venous pressure) is classically described but present in a minority; a high index of suspicion in the appropriate context is essential.

Pulsus paradoxus (an exaggerated inspiratory fall in systolic pressure greater than 10 mmHg) reflects enhanced ventricular interdependence and is a key bedside sign, though it may be absent in aortic regurgitation, atrial septal defect, severe hypotension or regional tamponade.
The jugular venous pressure shows a preserved or prominent systolic x descent with an attenuated or absent diastolic y descent, distinguishing tamponade from constrictive pericarditis.

Echocardiography demonstrates early diastolic right ventricular collapse (specific) and late diastolic/systolic right atrial collapse (sensitive), a dilated non-collapsing inferior vena cava and exaggerated respiratory variation in transvalvular Doppler inflow.
Low-voltage QRS complexes and electrical alternans on the ECG suggest a large effusion with the heart swinging within it.

Definitive treatment is drainage (echo-guided pericardiocentesis or surgical drainage); intravenous fluids may temporise but vasodilators and diuretics are harmful, and positive-pressure ventilation can precipitate cardiovascular collapse.
reference.pathophysiology: Accumulation of fluid, blood, pus or gas within the relatively non-distensible pericardial sac raises intrapericardial pressure. Once this pressure approaches and then exceeds the diastolic filling pressures of the cardiac chambers, transmural distending pressure falls and diastolic filling is progressively impeded, beginning with the lower-pressure right-sided chambers. As total cardiac volume becomes fixed, the ventricles compete for a shared volume across the interventricular septum (enhanced ventricular interdependence): inspiratory augmentation of right ventricular filling shifts the septum leftward and reduces left ventricular stroke volume, producing pulsus paradoxus. Compensatory tachycardia, increased adrenergic tone and elevated systemic venous pressure maintain output until, at a critical intrapericardial pressure, stroke volume and cardiac output fall precipitously, culminating in obstructive shock and pulseless electrical activity.
additionalDifferentials: massive pulmonary embolism with obstructive shock
severe acute right heart failure from any cause
additionalInvestigations: transthoracic echocardiography (chamber collapse, IVC plethora, Doppler respiratory variation)
12-lead ECG (low voltage, electrical alternans, sinus tachycardia)
chest radiograph (enlarged globular 'water-bottle' cardiac silhouette if effusion is large)
pericardial fluid analysis after drainage (cytology, culture, protein, LDH, adenosine deaminase)
CT or CMR when loculated or regional effusion, haemopericardium or aortic dissection is suspected
coagulation screen and full blood count
right heart catheterisation showing equalisation of diastolic pressures in equivocal cases
redFlags: hypotension with raised jugular venous pressure and tachycardia after cardiac procedure, trauma or in suspected aortic dissection
pulseless electrical activity or peri-arrest in a patient with known or suspected effusion
pulsus paradoxus greater than 10 mmHg with progressive breathlessness
echocardiographic right ventricular diastolic collapse with a dilated non-collapsing inferior vena cava
rapidly enlarging effusion following myocardial infarction (suggesting free wall rupture)
reference.prognosis: Prognosis depends chiefly on the underlying cause and the speed of recognition and drainage; promptly relieved tamponade has excellent haemodynamic recovery, whereas unrecognised tamponade from myocardial rupture or aortic dissection carries very high mortality. Malignant effusions frequently recur and portend a poor overall outlook.
pitfalls: Assuming a small effusion excludes tamponade; rapidly accumulating fluid causes compromise at low volumes.
Administering diuretics, vasodilators or nitrates, which reduce preload and can precipitate cardiovascular collapse.
Missing regional (loculated) tamponade after cardiac surgery, where localised clot compresses one chamber without the classic circumferential effusion.
Delaying drainage to await confirmatory imaging in a peri-arrest patient.
Attributing absent pulsus paradoxus to exclusion of tamponade, overlooking confounders such as aortic regurgitation or an atrial septal defect.
references: Braunwald's Heart Disease: A Textbook of Cardiovascular Medicine
ESC Guidelines for the Diagnosis and Management of Pericardial Diseases
Adler Y et al. Pericardial disease review, European Heart Journal
management: Relieve the tamponade urgently by echocardiographically guided pericardiocentesis, or surgical drainage where the effusion is loculated, haemorrhagic or traumatic
Support cardiac filling in the interim with intravenous fluids and, where needed, inotropic support, avoiding vasodilators and diuretics
Avoid positive-pressure ventilation where possible, as it further impairs venous return in the tamponading heart
Analyse drained pericardial fluid by cytology, culture and biochemistry and treat the underlying cause
Address a life-threatening cause directly, such as emergency surgery for myocardial rupture or aortic dissection
Monitor with serial echocardiography for re-accumulation after drainage
Create a pericardial window or consider pericardial sclerosis for recurrent malignant effusions, with oncology input
